blogs.title: Certifying Without Signatures: What Louisiana’s ‘Cancellation’ Statute Means
blogs.description: In Williams v. GoAuto, the Fifth Circuit held that a notice of cancellation can meet Louisiana’s statutory standard even without a signature. The analysis delves into the court’s reasoning, the historical use of the term “certifying,” and the practical implications for insurers and finance companies seeking compliant yet efficient cancellation procedures.

blogs.title: Private Carrier or Private Email? The Fifth Circuit’s Modern Interpretation of the Cancellation Statute
blogs.description: The Fifth Circuit treated an e‑mail transmission as a private carrier under § 9:3550(G)(3)(i), drawing on railroad analogies to justify modern communication methods. This post examines the doctrinal move, its fit with agency and carrier theory, and how it might affect the legal landscape as insurers and finance firms lean into automation.

blogs.title: Why the Fifth Circuit Won’t Certify: Lessons for Litigation and State‑Law Development
blogs.description: The plaintiffs requested certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court on the statutory interpretation of cancellation procedures. The Fifth Circuit declined, explaining that the lack of a defined Supreme Court precedent is insufficient. This analysis explores the court’s rationale, compares it to other circuits’ certification practices, and considers the procedural and policy consequences.

blogs.title: The Bottom Line for Premium‑Financed Insurance: Automating Cancellations and Consumer Protection
blogs.description: Williams v. GoAuto signals that automated, electronic cancellation systems can satisfy Louisiana’s strict statutory requirements. We assess the industry impact, discuss the balance between operational efficiency and good‑faith obligations, and consider how this ruling might shape consumer protections and future market practices.
